newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - Brazil phone bids to be unprecedented.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Brazil phone bids to be unprecedented.

text.p: Bidders seeking a prime piece of Brazil's cellular telephone concessions are going to pay prices unseen before in an emerging market, an adviser to one of the bidding groups said Monday.

Corrado Varoli, head of Latin American mergers and acquisitions at Morgan Stanley, told Reuters the bids submitted Monday would be higher because of the potential profits from the huge Brazilian market.

The price for the prize Sao Paulo metropolitan area, for example, is likely to be well above the $28-per-person winning offer when Panama auctioned its cellular concessions. The offer is the highest bid for such concessions in Latin America.

"You can expect significantly higher than that -- maybe two times Panama," said Varoli, who helped put together the bid submitted by AT&T Corp, Italy's Stet SpA and Brazil's Globo media group and Bradesco bank.
Market sources said the Sao Paulo city concession should fetch between $1 billion and $2 billion. The Rio de Janeiro state concession will follow with a likely winning bid of about $1 billion.
Fifteen consortiums embracing international and Brazilian companies submitted bids to Brazil's Communications Ministry to operate cellular telephone concessions.
The bidding is part of the reformist government's effort to end the state telephone monopoly. The groups submitted bids for nine of 10 regional concessions offered.
The government expects to raise about $100 billion over the next few years from privatization.
The winning bidders will compete in the regions against state-run Telebras SA, which has been starved of investment and is unable to keep up with exploding demand.
Telebras subscribers now pay about $2,000 and wait months for installation of a land line, with the cellular situation only slightly better, Varoli said.
One of the major attractions of the cellular offers for big international bidders was the puny threat seen from Telebras.
"It's a dream come true. It's a perfect competitor -- everybody is looking forward to that," Varoli said.
Brazil's other selling points were its newly stable economy and concentration of most potential telephone users in a few regions.
